name: Uma Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach beginner trombone on Mondays, play with the town band at weekends and record short brass lines for local events. I finished secondary school and still ask the senior player to catch my slips in a fast march.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part do you like, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the first clean note a child gets from the horn. I get tired of being told a town event is good exposure when the mortgage only takes money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the town band that AI can put rehearsal dates on a neat page, and I already use it for that. Somebody still has to count the brass in together when we play the square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have three months of expenses saved and my partner has steady plumbing work. A missed town concert would be irritating, not a missed mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep teaching beginner trombone on Mondays and playing with the band at the weekend. I already use AI every day for practice sheets, but I play each exercise before a pupil gets it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about future bookings but safe for the next few months. My better-paid partner’s work gives us a bit of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the outdoor concert was rained off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last outdoor concert was rained off, and we still got half the fee. I would ask the band leader to keep that cancellation term in the next agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your children see when you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children hear me practise the same hard bar over and over. A tidy page is not the same as getting the note out.

say: I would say **rehearsal dates** can get easier to share.
I would defend the band’s **live count-in** and cancellation fee.
think: Our **three-month cushion** and plumbing income protect the mortgage from one lost concert.
I still watch **town bookings** because fees cover family extras.
do: Keep **Monday trombone pupils** and weekend band work this season.
Ask the leader to keep the **half-fee cancellation term** in the next agreement.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about bookings, while household income stays sound.
S0.quote: A tidy page is not the same as getting the note out.
fieldNote: Her moderate **savings cushion** and partner’s steady plumbing pay support a mild mood.
Her daily **AI use** is established and checked by playing exercises herself.

steps.text: Keep Monday trombone pupils and weekend town band work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band leader that AI may write posters, arrange parts and book acts, but the players should see the paid calendar. I would ask for the live fee in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My short brass recordings for local events could lose buyers, perhaps a tenth of my income in a busy month. The town might also use generated tracks at smaller events.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the leader for three months of paid dates and test a new AI range checker on one trombone part only after a skilled player demonstrates it. In the first year I would play the part myself before sharing it and keep my Monday pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing my own recording fees, even with a few months saved. I can test a tool, but it cannot promise paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that range-checker safe enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not upload a pupil’s name or recording to a tool that stores it outside the school. I would test only a nameless part, and return to paper if the range is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the band offer if small events change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If small events use tracks, I would ask the band leader to offer a shorter live set rather than work unpaid. I would not spend our cushion to buy a new instrument on that guess.

say: I would ask for a **paid band calendar** before small events change.
I would offer **shorter live sets** at a fee rather than free performances.
think: My **brass recording fees** could shrink by a tenth in a busy month.
Generated **event tracks** might reduce small paid band dates.
do: Ask for **three paid months** of band dates next month.
Test the **AI range checker** only after a skilled demonstration, using a nameless part and keeping pupil data inside school.
Play the **trombone line** before sharing and return to paper if the range is wrong.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fees, with room to try a safer tool.
S1.quote: I can test a tool, but it cannot promise paid work.
fieldNote: Her new **AI trial** differs from daily practice-sheet use and includes a manual stop rule.
The **recording share** is meaningful to her even with a three-month buffer.

steps.text: Test AI range checker after skilled demo; keep pupil data inside school
Play nameless part before sharing and return to paper if range is wrong
Keep Monday trombone pupils while checking three months of band dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that AGI by 2028 could write every part, but the town still needs players for a live march. I would ask for the next festival roster before rehearsing unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my recording clips to go in 2028, and the town may buy fewer short live sets then. Robots for hands-on playing arrive around 2031. A cheap track can displace us before a robot plays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would collect my recording invoices and ask the town arts office about its paid beginner workshops. If AGI cuts band dates after 2028, I would apply for an open music-room aide post only if it accepts secondary school education and the hours fit pickup; I would keep trombone pupils while applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious because I expect part of my income to disappear, but three months saved lets us search. I would not take an unpaid workshop as a substitute for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any town workshop offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town post must be advertised and paid, and I would ask for the job description before applying. My partner can collect the children some days, but not every late afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner the recording number first, then agree that two months of savings stay untouched. We can cut a family outing before we cross that floor.

say: I would demand a **paid festival roster** before more rehearsals.
I would say a **live town march** still needs players.
think: My **recording clips** likely disappear in 2028 before 2031 stage robots.
Town **short-set fees** may shrink before a robot plays.
do: Ask the **town arts office** about paid beginner workshops this week.
Apply for an **open paid aide post** after 2028 cuts only if education and pickup fit.
Cut a **family outing** before household savings fall below two months.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected clip loss, with a short household search window.
S2.quote: A cheap track can displace us before a robot plays.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **2028 thinking loss** from around-2031 robot capability.
The town job requires **advertised pay and qualification**, plus pickup fit, while two months of savings stay untouched.

steps.text: Apply for advertised paid aide post if band dates fall, education and pickup fit
Keep trombone pupils while applying for the town post
Cut family outings before savings fall below two months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the town band that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to teach younger brass players. I would ask the band to fund a paid trainee place rather than expect a child to carry instruments for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recording clips may end by 2031, but I could run a better beginner class by then. Robots around 2034 might play the march, though I do not know whether a town would want that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would ask the school for a paid group-teaching workshop with a senior tutor if the hours fit pickup. If the tutor approves me, I would take a six-pupil group only if the school funds preparation and provides staff; in the first year after 2031 I would keep it while those conditions and paid enrollment hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about clip fees until the class pays. Five years lets me test a paid beginner trombone class, not count pupils who have not enrolled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school will not pay for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still learning to hear six instruments at once. If the school will not pay for the workshop, I would keep the one-to-one lessons and practise with the band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a band trainee do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainee could help set out stands and learn a part under supervision. I would ask for a small fee in the band budget, not call free lifting an apprenticeship.

say: I would ask for a **paid trainee place** in the band.
I would tell the town to keep **young brass players** learning.
think: My **recording clips** may end in 2031 before 2034 stage robots.
A **six-pupil class** could replace some fees if school conditions hold.
do: Seek a **paid tutor workshop** this autumn only if school funding and pickup fit.
Keep a **six-pupil group** after 2031 only with approval, paid preparation, staff, enrollment and workable pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** until the group produces real paid income.
S3.quote: Five years lets me test a paid beginner trombone class, not count pupils who have not enrolled.
fieldNote: Her route to group teaching requires **funded training** and a senior tutor’s explicit approval before six pupils arrive.
The post-2031 class still needs **staff and preparation pay**, enrolled pupils and workable pickup.

steps.text: Attend senior tutor workshop only if school pays and pickup fits
Keep six-pupil group after 2031 only with approval, paid preparation, staff, enrollment and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to learn useful work and keep playing together. I would ask the town to pay live players for events it still runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 a paid beginner group might replace recording clips, though it needs a school that keeps hiring. Robots around 2039 may play town events, but the next few years still have real band dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would save a portion of each paid event fee after the mortgage and food are covered, adding to our three-month cushion. In the first year after 2036 I would compare band and school pay, and apply for an advertised town aide post only if both fall and the job fits my schooling and pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the distant stage question. Our current pay and three months saved make next year manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What reserve would you aim for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would aim for six months of expenses by 2036 if paid events keep coming. I would not count a free parade in that savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that practice and a fair fee belong together. Love for music does not mean working without pay.

say: I would ask for **paid live players** at town events.
I would tell my children **practice and fair pay** belong together.
think: A paid **beginner group** may replace clip income by 2036.
Possible **2039 robots** do not threaten next year’s booked band dates.
do: Save part of each **paid event fee** after mortgage and food this year.
Apply for an **advertised town aide post** after 2036 only if both incomes fall and schooling and pickup fit.
Keep **paid town band dates** while organisers continue running live events.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later stage work, while current pay and savings hold.
S4.quote: Love for music does not mean working without pay.
fieldNote: Her reserve goal is **six months** only if paid town dates continue.
A later job search requires **advertised pay and qualification**, plus workable child pickup.

steps.text: Add paid event fees to cushion toward six months after mortgage and food

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because clip fees could vanish before a paid school role is open. A written festival roster, a qualifying paid aide post and time to keep two months saved would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the youngest player carrying the stands. A town cannot call its band local pride and pay it with applause.

headlineQuote: A town cannot call its band local pride and pay it with applause.
portrait: At **43**, Uma is a junior trombonist with secondary school education, two children, a mortgage and three months saved.
Her partner’s **plumbing pay** steadies the household, while recordings and town events add meaningful fees.
She uses **AI daily** for practice sheets and tests new tools only with demonstrations, nameless scores and her own playing.
She favours **paid apprenticeships** and qualified town work, adding savings only from real paid dates.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase clip fees before a qualifying paid town post opens.
whatWouldHelp: A **written roster**, qualifying aide post and protected savings floor would give Uma time to replace fees.
